chunks: Characterizing GPU performance. The question: How do you characterize GPU performance?
To characterize GPU performance, you measure three things: compute (how many operations per second it can do), memory (how many bytes per second it can move), and efficiency (work per watt).
Then you check which limit your workload actually hits. For graphics, you also look at frame time. Peak numbers say what the chip could do, not what your program gets.
Picture a factory with fast workers inside and one narrow loading door for materials. If each product needs little material, the workers are the limit.
If each product needs a lot, the door is the limit, and hiring more workers changes nothing. A GPU is like that.
Kernels that do little arithmetic per byte are limited by the memory "door".
Left of the orange ridge, performance rises linearly with intensity because bytes are the bottleneck; adding cores does nothing there.
Right of it, the flat roof is the compute peak. SAXPY sits far down the slope at 0. 24% of peak, a large tiled matrix multiply sits on the roof.
FLOPS: floating-point operations per second. A fused multiply-add (a multiply and an add done in one step) counts as 2.
Memory bandwidth: bytes per second between the GPU and its memory. Arithmetic intensity: operations done per byte of memory traffic.
Roofline model: attainable speed is the smaller of peak compute and bandwidth times intensity. Frame time: time to draw one frame.
Worst-case frames show stutter that average FPS (frames per second) hides.
Take 80 clusters of 128 lanes (small arithmetic units) at 1. 7 gigahertz. Peak is 80 times 128 times 2 times 1. 7 gigahertz about 34. 8 TFLOPS.
A 256-bit memory bus at 16 Gb/s per pin gives 256 times 16 over 8 equals 512 GB/s.
Now run y equals ax plus y : it does 2 operations per 12 bytes moved, which is 1/6 operation per byte.
The memory limit gives 512 times 10 to the 9 over 6 about 85 GFLOPS, about 0. 24% of peak. That is the whole idea: find which limit binds.
"I'd look at compute, memory and efficiency. Peak FLOPS is SMs times lanes times two times clock, about 35 TFLOPS for a typical card.
Memory bandwidth is bus width times data rate over eight, say 512 GB/s. The ratio, the ridge point of the roofline, tells me whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound.
For graphics I add fill rate and frame-time percentiles. Then performance per watt and achieved versus peak, measured on my real workload including transfers."
Quick check. A kernel has arithmetic intensity 0. 5 FLOP/B on a GPU with 512 GB/s bandwidth and 34. 8 TFLOPS peak. What limits it and what is the attainable performance?
